newsitem.title: GERMANY: German parliament rejects move to limit Iran ties.
newsitem.headline: German parliament rejects move to limit Iran ties.

text.p: The German parliament on Friday dismissed Iran's claim that Bonn exerts political influence over German courts, but stopped short of agreeing to opposition demands to curtail exports and diplomatic ties with Tehran.

The move coincided with the arrival in Bonn of a letter from Iranian President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, who has said he wants to prevent relations from worsening over the case of three Iranian dissidents and a translator murdered in Berlin in 1992.
The German lower house approved a motion saying it could not accept threats made by Iranian demonstrators against the Berlin prosecutor, who accused Tehran of ordering the dissidents' assassination.
And it rejected accusations from Tehran that the trial was an example of political justice.

But the house threw out a resolution proposed by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) and Greens which would have urged the government to freeze any arms-related exports to Iran and limit contacts to the bare diplomatic necessities.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's office declined to comment on the content of Rafsanjani's letter, a reply to a note Kohl sent last week expressing concern about bilateral ties and assuring Rafsanjani that German courts were not subject to political influence.

Rafsanjani had said after receiving the letter that the German government was under U.S. and Israeli pressure, but that he hoped the bilateral friendship would continue and Bonn would prevent tensions getting out of control.
However, a senior cleric appeared to be adding to tensions on Friday when he said Iranians would not tolerate German accusations that Tehran had ordered political killings.

"The (Iranian) people are ready to see themselves wounded and shot at but they are not ready to tolerate any insult to their sanctities," Ayatollah Ahmad Jannati said in a mass prayer sermon broadcast live on state-run Tehran radio.
"You saw Salman Rushdie's fate after that insult and rudeness," Jannati said.

Rushdie, a British novelist, has lived in hiding since 1989 when Iran's late spiritual leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini ordered his killing for allegedly blaspheming against Islam in his novel "The Satanic Verses".

"We shall strongly insist on our positions and values and will not surrender to any judge or court," Jannati, a senior cleric known for his fiery rhetoric, told worshippers gathered at Tehran University.
In Berlin, the Iranian charged with masterminding the 1992 assassinations said he had felt condemned from the start of the three-year trial.

"I can't have been the ringleader and the prosecutor's office knows it," Kazem Darabi told Berlin's Info Radio. "The prosecution hasn't come up with a single convincing piece of evidence that I knew or even suspected the slightest thing about the killings."
In addition to Darabi four Lebanese men are on trial for the murders.
